lesson_title: The Colours Were Hiding in Sunlight
hook_text: A rainbow does not paint colour onto the sky. Every one of those colours was already inside the sunlight on your back.
clip_script: A storm rolls off over Pretoria, the Sun breaks through low behind you, and an arch of colour appears. Where do the colours come from? Isaac Newton found out with a prism in a dark room. Sunlight went in white and came out as a band of colours. He put one colour through a second prism and it stayed the same colour, and he put all the colours back together into white. So white light is a mixture. When light enters glass or water at a slant, it slows and bends: refraction. Violet slows most and bends most, red bends least, so the colours fan out: dispersion. Every raindrop does this, bending, bouncing off its back and bending again. With the Sun behind you, drops at forty-two degrees send you red, and drops at forty send you violet. That is why red is always on the outside.
visual_style: A whiteboard storm cloud with a rainbow, then a prism splitting a white ray into a fan of colours, then a zoom into one raindrop showing light bending, reflecting and bending out.
pacing: An inviting opening, a crisp experiment, then a satisfying explanation.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and make a rainbow with a hosepipe.
